headline: NATO will hold its nuclear drill as planned

sources.title: NATO presses ahead with 'Steadfast Noon' nuclear drill after Russia's nuclear warning (Associated Press)
NATO Launching Nuclear Drills After Putin's Baltic Sea Nuke Warning (Newsweek)
NATO to hold nuclear drills as tensions with Russia escalate (Ukrainska Pravda)

chunks.text: NATO says its yearly [[nuclear exercise]] will {{go ahead}} [[as planned]]. On October 8, 2026, NATO officials said the drill, called Steadfast Noon, will start in Italy on October 13. Aircraft from 17 [[member countries]] could take part. The news came weeks after Russia [[issued a warning]] about nuclear weapons. NATO says it has not {{put the exercise off}} and will {{stick to}} its usual schedule. A senior official said there is no need to worry.

chunks.text: In late September, Russia warned NATO against trying to {{cut off}} Kaliningrad. This Russian [[territory]] on the Baltic Sea sits between Poland and Lithuania, two NATO members. Russia's [[embassy]] in Ireland said Russia would be ready to use all its weapons, including nuclear ones, to defend the region. [[Tensions]] have {{built up}} since a NATO exercise near Kaliningrad in August. Some European countries accuse Russia of {{carrying out}} [[sabotage]], which Russia denies.

The police carried out a search of the house. The army carried out a rescue after the storm. Several European countries accuse Russia of carrying out sabotage, and Russia denies it.

chunks.text: NATO officials have {{played down}} any link between the drill and [[current world events]]. They say it does not {{single out}} any country. The exercise {{goes back}} more than a decade and is held at about the same time every year. In past years, planes that can carry nuclear weapons have taken part. No real nuclear [[warheads]] or [[live ammunition]] are used. Most of the drill will happen near Italy, far from Russia.

[[Ground crews]] will practice loading and [[refueling]] aircraft. The head of NATO says such drills help protect peace and [[deter]] attacks. The senior official said a [[predictable]] exercise helps prevent mistakes. She added that NATO has not {{picked up on}} any big changes in Russia's forces that would [[cause alarm]].

mainIdea.s: NATO will hold its yearly nuclear drill in Italy this October, even after a recent Russian warning. The alliance calls it routine training that keeps its forces ready and targets no country.
mainIdea.why: NATO says the drill will go ahead as planned. Officials say it trains forces and does not single out any country.

mainIdea.s: NATO is moving its nuclear drill close to Kaliningrad this year as an answer to Russia. Officials say the move shows that threats from Moscow will not change any of the alliance's plans.
mainIdea.why: Close, but most of the drill will happen near Italy, far from Russia. NATO has played down any link to current world events.

mainIdea.s: Russia has started its own yearly nuclear training near the Baltic Sea, using ships from its main navy base. Leaders in Moscow say about two thousand troops will join over the next two weeks.
mainIdea.why: This story is about NATO's own yearly drill. It goes back more than a decade and will start in Italy on October 13.

lines.text: Did you see that NATO's nuclear drill is {{going ahead}} next week?
Even after Russia's warning? I thought they might {{put it off}}.
No, they say it's [[business as usual]]. It happens at the same time every year.
How long have they been doing it?
It {{goes back}} more than a decade. It happens [[like clockwork]] every October.
And what was Russia's warning about?
Kaliningrad. Russia told NATO not to try to {{cut off}} that region.
It is. Tensions have {{built up}} since a NATO exercise near there in August.
So how is NATO handling it?
Officials are {{playing down}} any link. They say the drill doesn't {{single out}} any country.
Mostly near Italy, far from Russia. And no real nuclear weapons are used.
Good. Right now, it's important for everyone to [[keep a cool head]].
A NATO official said something similar. She said there's no need to worry.
Did they {{spell out}} what they'll practice?
No. But she said NATO hasn't {{picked up on}} any big changes in Russia's forces.
